newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli government stable after crisis - spokesman.
newsitem.headline: Israeli government stable after crisis - spokesman.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu intends to turn to important matters of state now that he has quelled a three-week cabinet crisis, his spokesman said on Tuesday.

But analysts said that while Netanyahu had solved one cabinet crisis by strengthening Foreign Minister David Levy's hand in peacemaking, he fanned another by snubbing ultra-hawk Ariel Sharon's bid for more power in the government.
"The government is going to act on the really important matters now that this affair has come to an end," said spokesman Shai Bazak. "The coalition is going to be really stable now."

Israeli-Palestinian peace talks have been on hold since Netanyahu sent bulldozers in March to break ground for a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem. The PLO demands Netanyahu stop the work before negotiations can resume. He has refused.
Netanyahu appointed lawyer Yaacov Neeman on Monday to the vacant post of finance minister at the expense of Sharon, thought to have been a sure bet to win the Treasury.
The prime minister was expected to ask parliament on Wednesday at 10 a.m. (0700 GMT) to approve the posting along with the appointment of loyalist Michael Eitan as science minister.

Netanyahu also decided to move weekly cabinet meetings from Friday to Sunday to accommodate religious cabinet members who complained long Friday meetings made it difficult to get home in time for the sabbath.

The prime minister bowed to Levy's demand to grant him formal control of peace talks with the Palestinians and do away with an inner ministerial forum on key policy issues on which Sharon demanded a seat.

"Netanyahu succeeded in creating another ominous rival in the form of Mr Sharon," political scientist Ehud Sprinzak told Reuters. "Sharon is a powerful force within Netanyahu's Likud party. This could create serious problems for in the long run."

Sharon, a champion of Jewish settlements in occupied lands whose potential ascent rattled Arabs and Israel's key ally the United States, praised Neeman's appointment and laughed off reports he felt betrayed.
"Really now, you must be joking," chortled the burly ex-general who continues to hold his post as national infrastructure minister.
Netanyahu, tossing Sharon an olive branch, said he would seek his advice on peace moves.

The Israeli leader suffered two key Likud cabinet defections during his first year in office. Right-winger Benny Begin resigned as science minister in January and Dan Meridor vacated the finance ministry in June.
Some analysts backed Bazak's prediction the cabinet changes could put some life into stalled peace moves with the PLO.

"We have now just about turned the corner on the domestic political deadlock. This will mark the start of more serious talks with the Palestinians, where we are still left with more substantive deadlock," said Gerald Steinberg of the Begin-Sadat Centre for Strategic Studies at Bar-Ilan University.

The clock is now ticking towards September, when Israel is due to implement the second of three promised troop withdrawals from West Bank rural areas -- although the Palestinians rejected Israel's first pullback offer as too stingy.
Others were sceptical Netanyahu's new cabinet, more loyalist with the addition of Neeman and Eitan, could meet the September deadline.
"Nothing has changed. They haven't changed their stances and it is built into this government that it responds only to outside pressures," said political scientist Meron Benvenisti.
"It's just time to wait for the next crisis."
